themes.name: Memory Supply Chain
themes.whatChanged: The memory shortage stopped being cyclical and started looking structural. Data centres now consume roughly 70% of all memory produced globally, and the three makers who control 95%+ of DRAM have redirected capacity toward high-bandwidth memory for AI accelerators — starving everything else. SK Hynix's CEO said in July the shortage will likely persist past 2030. Micron's CEO said they can fill only half to two-thirds of demand into 2027.

dataPoints.label: Mobile DRAM Q/Q ask
dataPoints.detail: Samsung and Micron sought >80%; SK Hynix opened 55-60%

dataPoints.label: Datacentre share of memory output
dataPoints.detail: of all memory chips produced worldwide

portfolioImpact.reason: This is the thesis, and it is playing out — pricing power across every name on your list simultaneously.
HBM demand is the direct cause of the shortage; NVDA sits upstream of it as the demand driver.
Buys mobile DRAM at enormous scale. An 80% input price rise is real gross-margin pressure they cannot fully pass to consumers.
Server memory costs rise, but Azure pricing absorbs it and AI revenue growth outweighs the input hit.

themes.watch: Micron earnings for guidance on how far into 2027 the shortage extends, and whether any maker announces new non-HBM capacity.

themes.name: Fed & Rates
themes.whatChanged: The gap between producer and consumer inflation has become the thing to watch. PPI is running at 10.1% year over year against CPI at 3.7% — producers are absorbing cost increases they have not yet passed on. That gap closes one of two ways: margins compress, or consumer prices catch up. Neither is good for a Fed hoping to cut.

dataPoints.label: PPI
dataPoints.detail: year over year, June — the outlier

portfolioImpact.reason: Cash keeps earning while rates stay elevated. The longer cuts are delayed, the longer this holds.
Equity valuations are priced for cuts. A PPI-driven delay removes a support the market has already banked.
The most liquidity-sensitive thing you own. Higher-for-longer is a direct headwind.
Long-duration cash flows are rate-sensitive, but earnings strength has been offsetting it so far.

themes.watch: Next CPI print, and whether PPI decelerates. If PPI stays double-digit while CPI sits near 3.7%, something has to give.

themes.name: AI Infrastructure
themes.whatChanged: Hyperscalers reaffirmed aggressive capex plans on earnings, which resolved the capex-sustainability scare that had knocked chip names down mid-week. Around 86% of S&P 500 companies reporting have beaten expectations. The spending cycle is intact for now.

dataPoints.label: TSMC Q2 profit
dataPoints.detail: record quarter; 2026 revenue growth guided above 40%

portfolioImpact.reason: Direct beneficiary. Hyperscaler capex converts almost mechanically into NVDA revenue.
Both a spender and a seller — Azure AI revenue is the return on that capex.
Heavily weighted to exactly these names, which cuts both ways but is working now.

themes.watch: Whether capex guidance holds through the next quarter, or any hyperscaler signals digestion. That is the single point of failure for this theme.

themes.name: Tariffs
themes.whatChanged: Beijing and Washington floated cutting roughly $30bn in tariffs, with China's Ministry of Commerce seeking public input — an early procedural step, not an agreement. Meanwhile semiconductor and hardware firms with China exposure remain the most tariff-sensitive corner of the market.

portfolioImpact.reason: Largest China manufacturing exposure you own. Genuine upside if this lands, genuine risk if talks reverse — currently unresolved in both directions.
China export restrictions matter more to NVDA than tariffs per se; this proposal does not address them.
Tariff de-escalation is broadly supportive of Chinese and Asian equities, which anchor most EM indices.

themes.watch: Whether the comment period produces an actual schedule. Until then this is noise.

themes.name: Defense & Geopolitics
themes.whatChanged: The Hormuz de-escalation from early August reversed. Strikes between the US and Iran intensified again in early September, and vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has effectively collapsed — from 100+ ships a day to roughly 5-12. The IEA has called it the largest oil supply disruption in the history of the global oil market, on the order of 20 million barrels a day removed. WTI has moved from the high-$80s to $97+/bbl in under two weeks; Brent is trading near $104-105. Forecasts diverge sharply on what happens next: Goldman Sachs’ base case has Brent easing back toward $85, while Rystad Energy’s scenario puts it above $140 with global recession risk attached.

dataPoints.detail: up from the high-$80s in under two weeks

dataPoints.label: Supply removed
dataPoints.detail: IEA: largest disruption in the history of the global oil market

dataPoints.label: Price forecast range
dataPoints.detail: Goldman Sachs base case vs. Rystad Energy recession scenario

portfolioImpact.reason: Oil feeds directly into CPI/PPI — the same PPI-CPI gap already flagged in the Fed & Rates theme — and a fresh inflation input makes a near-term rate cut less likely. Cash keeps earning while that persists.
Exposed on two fronts: an oil-driven inflation resurgence delays the cut equities are priced for, and the Rystad scenario attaches outright recession risk if the Strait stays effectively closed.
The most liquidity-sensitive holding here — a risk-off shock this size, on top of an already-elevated-rate environment, is a direct headwind, not the mixed read a de-escalation would have been.

themes.watch: Whether the Strait reopens to normal traffic or the closure persists — Goldman’s $85 base case and Rystad’s $140+/recession scenario diverge entirely on that question. The Sep 17 FOMC decision (already tracked below) is now also a referendum on whether the Fed treats this inflation input as transitory or persistent.

themes.name: Emerging Markets
themes.whatChanged: China's equity market rallied on AI demand while its factories contracted — July manufacturing PMI fell into contraction for the first time since February. Brazil is cutting rates into fast-falling inflation. Mexico's GDP is rebounding on nearshoring. India's RBI was expected to hold at 5.25%.

portfolioImpact.reason: Your only direct EM exposure. China dominates most EM indices, and China is currently two contradictory stories at once — strong exports, weak domestic demand.

themes.watch: Whether China's PMI contraction persists into August. One month is noise; two is a trend.

catalysts.label: NVIDIA to acquire Hugging Face ($12.93B)
catalysts.why: Direct expansion of NVDA's AI platform reach into model distribution — 18M+ developers, 3M+ models on the platform today. NVIDIA committed Hugging Face stays open (no NVIDIA-compute requirement, continued multi-cloud/multi-accelerator support), so this reads as a distribution/ecosystem play rather than a lock-in move.
